claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist as a single-phase, chemically disordered solid solution without pre-existing short-range order.
The low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi arise from its failure to develop stress-induced short-range order during mechanical loading.
Mechanical deformation can induce short-range order in some multi-principal-element alloys.
The extent of mechanically induced short-range order can depend on loading rate.
Stress-induced partial ordering normally impedes dislocation glide.
CoCrFeNiTi remains chemically disordered under room-temperature compression to approximately 5% plastic strain.
The absence of stress-induced ordering permits freer dislocation glide in CoCrFeNiTi.
Freer dislocation glide caused by absent ordering leads to lower work hardening, hardness, and strength.
Diffraction peak shifts and broadening can be used to track lattice-strain evolution during compression.
Emerging superlattice reflections would indicate stress-induced short-range ordering.
During compression, CoCrFeNiTi will exhibit continuous diffraction-peak shifts and broadening.
No new superlattice reflections will appear during compression of CoCrFeNiTi.
Compressed CoCrFeNiTi will have a low work-hardening rate consistent with relatively uninhibited dislocation motion.
Other high-entropy or multi-principal-element alloys provide examples of stress-induced short-range ordering.
The cited stress-induced-ordering benchmark operates under loading conditions similar to room-temperature compression at approximately 0.001 per second.
The proposed mechanism is specifically applicable to single-phase equimolar CoCrFeNiTi under room-temperature uniaxial compression and moderate plastic strain.
The mechanism may change at low temperature or at different strain rates.
Conventional X-ray diffraction may lack sensitivity to subtle or incipient short-range order.
